# Evaluation and Observability {#sec-eval-practice}

An evaluation begins with an **evaluation release**: a named decision about one
version of a complete system. Before anything runs, the release fixes the
system fingerprint (the revisions of every component that can change behavior),
the decision claim, the target population, the critical slices (named subsets
of cases, such as one language, that are judged separately), the
release gate, and the rollback target. The result tells an owner whether to
merge, canary, ramp, stop, or continue operating the system.

This chapter turns the measurement principles from @sec-benchmarks,
@sec-statistical-reliability, @sec-human-evaluation-rubrics,
@sec-judging-holistic, @sec-factuality-grounding, @sec-evaluating-agents, and
@sec-operational-evaluation into an operating protocol. The subject is the
running application, including the serving layer (@sec-serving-stack), model
gateway (@sec-wiring-stack), retrieval (@sec-retrieval-practice), agents
(@sec-agents-practice), and any fine-tuned model (@sec-training-practice).

## Freeze the release contract

The **release contract** records the answers to six questions before any result
is visible.

| Contract field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | Merge, shadow, canary, ramp, rollback, or continued operation; owner and expiry |
| System fingerprint | Model revision, prompt revision, retrieval snapshot, tool schema, policy revision, parser, and gateway configuration |
| Claim | Decision claim, metric direction, independent unit, target population, time window, and case weight |
| Evidence | Dataset revision and provenance, scoring protocol, repeated-trial policy, critical slices, and uncertainty method |
| Gate | Hard constraints, non-inferiority margins, risk ceilings, latency and cost budgets, and stop rules |
| Recovery | Last-known-good revision, rollback trigger, rollback procedure, and requalification trigger |

The fingerprint lists component revisions because a prompt, index, tool
description, safety policy, parser, route, or provider alias can change behavior
while the model name and the application version stay the same. Each evaluation
result is therefore bound to immutable component digests. Without that binding,
production ML systems accumulate hidden dependencies and failure modes that
appear when the world around them changes [@sculley2015debt; @breck2017mltest].

### Three different jobs

Evaluation asks whether declared evidence supports a decision about a fixed
system. In a running system, @gls-observability records enough structured events
to reconstruct what the system did. Monitoring compares measurements with
thresholds over time and routes exceptions to an owner. The three jobs can share
storage and instrumentation, but each answers a different question.

A trace is partial evidence of what the system did; it is not a label and not
ground truth. Instrumentation can be absent, sampled, dropped, redacted, or
wrong, and a quality score can also be wrong. Keeping traces and scores apart
prevents a telemetry export failure from looking like an improvement in product
quality.

## Choose the tooling

The tools divide along the same jobs, and the first division is between
capability evaluation and application evaluation. A capability harness
measures a model: it compares checkpoints, validates a fine-tune
(@sec-training-practice), or reproduces a published benchmark number. An
application evaluation tool measures the running system, one prompt, retrieval
pipeline, and agent, against the release contract. Observability platforms
record traces, and most of them now also score traces and manage datasets, so
one product often serves several jobs while the jobs themselves stay separate.

| Tool | What it is | License | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| lm-evaluation-harness (EleutherAI) | Harness for few-shot evaluation on many academic benchmarks, with reproducible task configurations | MIT | Measuring a model's capability reproducibly |
| Inspect (UK AISI) | Framework for model and agent evaluations with tool use, multi-turn tasks, sandboxes, and model-graded scoring; Inspect Evals collects ready-made tasks | MIT | Agentic and safety evaluations |
| Promptfoo | Configuration-driven CLI for application evaluations and red-teaming: assertions, model judges, model comparison, and adversarial scans | MIT, plus a commercial enterprise tier | Application evaluations and security tests that run in CI |
| DeepEval (Confident AI) | pytest-style framework with judge, retrieval, agent, and safety metrics, including G-Eval and DAG metrics | Apache 2.0, plus the Confident AI cloud | Regression tests on model output written as unit tests |
| Ragas | Retrieval metrics such as faithfulness and context precision and recall | Apache 2.0 | Scoring a retrieval pipeline, often through another framework |
| MLflow | Tracing and evaluation for GenAI applications inside the MLflow platform | Apache 2.0 | Teams standardized on MLflow or Databricks |

| Platform | What it is | License and deployment | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Langfuse | Tracing, prompt management, evaluations, and datasets | MIT outside its enterprise directories; self-hosted or cloud | A self-hostable observability and evaluation stack |
| Arize Phoenix | Tracing and evaluation built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, runnable locally | Elastic License 2.0; self-hosted, with a commercial cloud | OpenTelemetry-native tracing without an account |
| Opik (Comet) | Tracing, judge metrics, datasets, and dashboards | Apache 2.0; self-hosted or cloud | Another self-hostable option |
| LangSmith (LangChain) | Managed tracing, evaluation, and prompt platform | Proprietary service | Teams on LangChain or LangGraph that want a managed platform |
| Braintrust | Evaluation-first platform with experiments, scoring, tracing, and a prompt playground | Proprietary service | Product teams that want evaluation and tracing in one interface |
| W&B Weave | Tracing, evaluation, and version tracking in the Weights & Biases ecosystem | Apache 2.0 SDK; hosted service | Teams already using Weights & Biases |

The tables follow each project's documentation or repository
[@lmevalharness2026; @inspectai2026; @inspectevals2026; @promptfoo2026docs;
@deepeval2026; @deepeval2026judge; @ragas2026repo; @mlflow2026genai;
@langfuse2026repo; @phoenix2026repo; @opik2026; @langsmith2026;
@braintrust2026; @wandb2026weave]. Under both sits the instrumentation
substrate. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define vendor-neutral
`gen_ai.*` attributes for model, tool, and agent spans, metrics, and events
[@otel2026genaisemconv], and OpenInference supplies conventions that complement
them together with automatic instrumentation for model SDKs, agent frameworks,
and retrieval libraries, emitting to any OpenTelemetry backend
[@openinference2026repo]. Instrumenting once against this substrate is what
lets a team change backends without re-instrumenting, which matters in a
category whose products change owners.

Four questions narrow the application tooling.

| Question | Options | When they fit |
|---|---|---|
| Where do evaluations live? | Promptfoo (configuration and CLI) or DeepEval (pytest) | Evaluations live in the repository and gate merges without an external account |
| | Braintrust or LangSmith | People who do not write code curate datasets and compare runs in a hosted interface |
| Who operates the platform? | Langfuse, Phoenix, or Opik, self-hosted | Data residency, cost control, or vendor neutrality justify operating it |
| | LangSmith, Braintrust, or Confident AI | The team pays so that it does not operate one |
| How is the code instrumented? | OpenTelemetry with OpenInference | One instrumentation reaches many backends |
| | A vendor SDK | Faster setup, at the cost of coupling code to one vendor |
| Is red-teaming in scope? | Promptfoo | Built-in adversarial scans for prompt injection, jailbreaks, and data leakage |

A team shipping one or two features that wants a continuous loop without a
platform team can start from open, self-hostable, OpenTelemetry-native parts:
Langfuse for tracing, Promptfoo for application evaluations and red-teaming in
CI with DeepEval where pytest-style metrics fit better, Inspect or
lm-evaluation-harness for capability evaluation, and OpenTelemetry GenAI spans
emitted through OpenInference. A managed platform can replace the tracing and
evaluation parts later without new instrumentation. A team already standardized
on MLflow or on Weights & Biases uses the evaluation features of that platform
in preference to adding another vendor.

## Build an evaluation dataset

An **evaluation case** is a versioned input plus the environment, expected
behavior, allowed actions, label provenance, privacy status, and slice metadata
needed to score it. The case also records whether it came from a designed
scenario, a public benchmark, a synthetic generator, expert review, or
production.

Production traffic is a selected sample, not a random draw from the target
population, and consent or another valid authority must cover its use. Before a trace enters any suite, it is redacted,
triaged, given an adjudicated expected behavior, deduplicated, and assigned to a
split. The splits serve three separate roles:

- a development suite for prompt, policy, and scorer iteration;
- a diagnostic suite for incidents, adversarial cases, and exploratory slices;
- a locked holdout, kept out of all iteration, for confirmation.

Cases are grouped by the unit that can leak information across splits: user,
tenant, conversation family, repository, source document, or time block.
Grouping happens before split assignment, and a search for exact and near
duplicates across splits follows it. If a holdout case, answer, label, or close
paraphrase influenced the prompt, retriever, judge, parser, or selection of the
candidate, it counts as contamination and is removed from confirmatory evidence
[@kapoor2023leakage].

### Cases and repeated trials

A **stochastic trial** is one run of one system on one evaluation case under a
recorded random seed and environment snapshot. Repeated trials of a case
estimate run-to-run variation, and repeated trials are not independent cases:
they add no new user, task, or document. Every timeout, refusal, parser failure,
tool error, and empty result stays in the record. Selecting the best attempt is
valid only when production uses that same selection policy.

The independent unit and case weight must follow the deployment claim. For a
conversation product, turns and spans are nested within a conversation. For a
repository assistant, files and tool calls may be nested within a repository
task. Sample size therefore counts independent units, not rows.

## Score behavior without hiding failure

Each criterion is scored with the most direct evidence available among five
kinds.

1. A **deterministic check** executes an invariant: schema validity,
   authorization, exact calculation, tool arguments, citation existence, or a
   latency ceiling. An output that parses can still be semantically wrong, so a
   passing check does not establish semantic correctness.
2. A **task or reference score** measures an observable outcome: tests passed,
   evidence retrieved, claims supported, trajectory completed, or user goal
   achieved.
3. A **human judgment** applies a criterion-separated rubric when expertise and
   context are required.
4. A **qualified model judge**, a language model that scores outputs and has
   passed the qualification described below, approximates a specific human or
   executable scoring protocol.
5. An **operational metric** measures availability, end-to-end latency, resource
   use, or cost. A separate security criterion measures policy violations and
   attack success.

These kinds of evidence are reported separately rather than collapsed into one
“quality” number. The report covers every predeclared slice, including
low-volume and high-risk slices, and records `pass`, `fail`, `invalid`, `error`,
`abstain`, and `fallback` as separate outcomes. A slice with too few cases to
decide is reported as unresolved rather than treated as safe, and an aggregate
gain does not offset a regression inside a slice. HELM's multi-metric,
multi-scenario design applies the same principle to benchmark evaluation
[@liang2022helm].

### Compare complete revisions

The comparison runs candidate system $B$ and baseline system $A$ on the same
cases in a compatible environment, using a score where higher is better. Here
$i$ indexes cases, $r$ indexes repeats, $R_i$ is the number of declared repeats
for case $i$, $s$ is the score, and $w_i$ is the predeclared case weight. The
paired change is estimated as

$$
\widehat{\Delta}
=
\frac{1}{\sum_i w_i}
\sum_i w_i
\left(
  \frac{1}{R_i}
  \sum_{r=1}^{R_i}
  \left(s_{ir}^{B}-s_{ir}^{A}\right)
\right).
$$

Here $s_{ir}^{B}$ is the candidate score and $s_{ir}^{A}$ is the baseline score
for the same case and repeat; $\widehat{\Delta}$ is their deployment-weighted
paired change. Both systems share the case, corpus snapshot, tool policy,
budgets, and scorer. The random seed is shared only when both implementations
interpret it the same way.

The report gives a confidence interval for this paired change. A bootstrap
interval (@sec-statistical-reliability) must resample cases, or the higher-level
user, conversation, repository, or document clusters named by the contract,
rather than their nested turns, spans, or repeats. A hierarchical bootstrap,
which resamples clusters and then units within them, can represent both case and
run variation. A row-wise bootstrap treats rows that share a deployment unit as
independent, which invents information and narrows the interval
[@efron1979bootstrap; @bouthillier2021variance].

The cell below measures how much. It simulates paired differences for 60 cases
with 8 repeated trials each, where the true change varies across cases by
`between` and each trial adds run noise `within`, and it computes a 95 percent
interval both ways. The case bootstrap is wider by close to the square root of
the design effect, $\sqrt{1+(R-1)\,\mathrm{ICC}}$, where $\mathrm{ICC}$, the
intraclass correlation, is the share of the variance that lies between cases.
Raising `R` to 32 narrows the row-wise interval further while the case interval
barely moves, because repeats add runs of the same cases and no new cases.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
cases, R = 60, 8               # independent cases, repeated trials per case
between, within = 0.15, 0.05   # spread of the true change across cases, run noise

effect = rng.normal(0.02, between, cases)                 # true change of B over A per case
d = effect[:, None] + rng.normal(0, within, (cases, R))   # paired differences s_B - s_A
B = 4000

rows = d.ravel()
row_boot = rng.choice(rows, (B, rows.size)).mean(axis=1)             # rows treated as independent
case_boot = d[rng.integers(0, cases, (B, cases))].mean(axis=(1, 2))  # whole cases resampled

w_row = np.subtract(*np.percentile(row_boot, [97.5, 2.5]))
w_case = np.subtract(*np.percentile(case_boot, [97.5, 2.5]))
icc = between**2 / (between**2 + within**2)
predicted = np.sqrt(1 + (R - 1) * icc)   # square root of the design effect
print(f"paired change {d.mean():+.3f}")
print(f"95% width, row-wise bootstrap {w_row:.3f}")
print(f"95% width, case bootstrap     {w_case:.3f}")
print(f"ratio {w_case / w_row:.2f}, predicted sqrt(1 + (R-1)*ICC) = {predicted:.2f}")
assert abs(w_case / w_row / predicted - 1) < 0.15
```
::::

### Predeclare the release gate

The full gate is in @sec-operational-evaluation; this section uses its
non-inferiority rule and hard constraints. Here $L_j$ denotes the lower
confidence bound for change $j$ (one criterion on one slice, oriented so that
higher is better), and $\delta_j$ denotes its non-inferiority margin, the largest
regression the gate tolerates. A release can require

$$
L_j \ge -\delta_j
\qquad
\text{for every required slice and criterion }j.
$$

The gate also requires every hard constraint to pass, for example zero
cross-tenant access, valid tool authorization, an upper risk bound below its
ceiling, and a tail-latency budget. No margin or confidence level is universal;
each follows from consequence, desired precision, sample design, and decision
cost. Confirmatory claims are prespecified, and searching many comparisons for a
favorable result requires a multiple-comparison correction
[@dror2018significance].

Observing no failures in a sample does not show that the risk is zero. When
critical events are rare, the report gives an upper uncertainty bound on their
rate; if that bound does not fall below the risk ceiling, the gate is
unresolved. A hard policy failure can remain a stop even when its estimated rate
is imprecise.

## Treat a model judge as an instrument

A model judge extends review capacity and is handled as a versioned measurement
instrument: its error rates are measured, by the protocol of
@sec-judging-holistic, before its scores count as evidence. The judge revision,
rubric revision, prompt, decoding settings (the sampling parameters that shape
its output), candidate order, output schema, and parser are frozen, and the
judge is qualified on a locked human-labeled set for each criterion and slice
where it will operate.

Qualification reports the confusion matrix (counts of each human label paired
with each judge label), false-pass and false-fail rates, abstentions, parser
errors, uncertainty, and disagreement with humans. A judge can favor a candidate
for its position, its length, or its resemblance to the judge's own outputs.
Swapping candidate order and
identifiers tests position bias; meaning-preserving padding tests verbosity
bias; generator-identifying and paraphrased outputs test self-preference.
Further tests cover repeated-run stability and prompt injection carried in the
candidate text. Research has documented position, verbosity, and
self-preference effects, so a judge from another model family counts as
independent only once that independence is tested
[@zheng2023judge; @wang2023large; @panickssery2024selfpreference].
G-Eval shows that rubric-guided judging can improve agreement with human ratings
on the tasks it studied; that result does not establish validity on other tasks
[@liu2023geval].

Cohen's kappa, introduced for human raters in @sec-human-evaluation-rubrics,
corrects observed categorical agreement for the agreement expected from the
marginal label frequencies, how often each rater uses each label
[@cohen1960kappa]. In confusion-matrix notation it is

$$
p_o=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{a\in\mathcal C}n_{aa},
\qquad
p_e=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{a\in\mathcal C}n_{a\cdot}n_{\cdot a},
\qquad
\kappa=\frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e}.
$$

Here $\mathcal C$ is the label set, $n_{ab}$ counts human label $a$ and judge
label $b$, $n$ is the number of cases, and the dotted subscripts are marginal
totals. Kappa measures agreement, not correctness or safety, and it changes with
the prevalence of each label. It is reported beside criterion-specific error
rates and confidence intervals; no kappa value serves as a universal trust
threshold.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
def cohen_kappa(matrix):
    total = sum(sum(row) for row in matrix)
    observed = sum(matrix[i][i] for i in range(len(matrix))) / total
    row_totals = [sum(row) for row in matrix]
    col_totals = [sum(matrix[r][c] for r in range(len(matrix)))
                  for c in range(len(matrix))]
    expected = sum(r * c for r, c in zip(row_totals, col_totals)) / total**2
    return observed, (observed - expected) / (1 - expected)

# Rows are human labels; columns are judge labels: [bad, good].
agreement, kappa = cohen_kappa([[16, 4], [18, 162]])
assert round(agreement, 2) == 0.89
assert round(kappa, 2) == 0.53
print(f"agreement={agreement:.2f}, kappa={kappa:.2f}")
```
::::

```{figure}
//| figure: judge-qualification
//| label: fig-evaluation-and-observability-judge-kappa
//| fig-cap: "The chapter's qualification example: human-labeled cases, rows the human label and columns the judge label, with the judge's false-pass and false-fail rates held fixed while the share of cases humans label good changes. It opens on the runnable matrix [[16, 4], [18, 162]]. As good cases approach 100%, raw agreement $p_o$ approaches the judge's accuracy on good cases, $\kappa$ falls toward 0, and the false-pass rate rests on fewer bad cases, so its 95% Wilson interval (shaded) widens. ## Promote production evidence carefully
```

Production cases added to the suite over time should extend its coverage
without contaminating it. A complaint, incident, judge disagreement, or unusual
trace enters a diagnostic queue first. An owner verifies use authority, removes
sensitive data, reconstructs the system fingerprint, decides whether the case is
reproducible, labels or adjudicates the expected behavior, deduplicates it, and
assigns a suite role. The case becomes a regression case only after these steps.

Two production samples are kept:

- a probability or stratified sample for estimating population behavior;
- a risk queue for incidents, rare failures, complaints, and uncertain cases.

The risk queue serves discovery. Its cases were selected because they looked
risky or unusual, so its average is not a population rate. For the inference
sample, the record includes each case's inclusion probability (the chance that
the sampler selected it), the assignment unit, nonresponse, and label delay.
User feedback, retries, and abandonment are selected observational signals, and
they do not identify the causal effect of a release. When the decision requires
a causal claim, it needs randomized, sticky assignment and valid exposure logs
[@kohavi2009experiments].


## Define the trace contract

A trace groups work that belongs to one distributed request or task. The trace
contract fixes the fields each span in it carries: a trace ID, span ID, parent
span when one exists, operation name, start and end times, status, and
attributes. A span event records a timestamped occurrence inside a span; a span
link connects causally related work that is not a parent-child edge. Queues,
fan-out, retries, and multi-agent work produce such relations.

For an AI operation, the span also records the immutable system fingerprint,
model and route, prompt and policy identifiers, retrieval and tool revisions,
input digest, output digest, usage, cache result, retry number, and evidence
IDs. Raw content is not required for correlation. OpenTelemetry provides general
trace semantics and evolving GenAI conventions, but custom attributes still need
a local schema and version [@otel2026trace; @otel2026genaisemconv].

W3C Trace Context propagates the `traceparent` identifier across service
boundaries [@w3c2021tracecontext]. Baggage carries application metadata along
with that context and is not a secret store, so credentials, personally
identifiable information, tenant content, and authorization grants never go into
it. Incoming context is validated because external callers can forge it.

### Minimize before export

Data classification happens at instrumentation time, and raw payload recording
is off by default. The pipeline must redact before export and may tokenize or
hash only when the threat model permits it. Access to sensitive content is
separate from ordinary trace access. Tenant isolation, purpose-bound roles, an
access log, retention limits, and tested deletion apply across the collector,
backend, cache, archive, and derived evaluation datasets. The telemetry path is
a data system and belongs inside the AI risk-management boundary
[@nist2023airmf].

Prompts, retrieved text, tool results, and model output are untrusted data. They
may contain indirect prompt injection (instructions planted in content the
system later reads) or instructions aimed at a later judge. An evaluator should
have no production write authority, secrets, network tools, or unbounded budget.

### Sampling changes the estimate

**Head sampling** decides near request start, usually from a fixed probability.
**Tail sampling** waits for outcome information and can retain errors, slow
requests, rare routes, or security events. Tail rules help diagnosis and, by
construction, oversample the outcomes they select. @fig-observability-sampling
measures that oversampling for an error rate.

A report of population rates records the inclusion probability of each sampling
stratum and computes a design-weighted estimate, which weights each retained
trace by the inverse of its inclusion probability. A stable probability sample
is kept alongside special retention for errors, rare slices, security signals,
and judge disagreement; without it, a dashboard over retained traces shows a
biased sample. Missing telemetry, collector queue depth, dropped spans, broken
parentage, and export failure are monitored as first-class rates, so that
unknown evidence is not silently counted as success.

```{figure}
//| figure: trace-sampling
//| label: fig-observability-sampling
//| fig-cap: "An illustrative population of 2,000 traces, one square each, with error rate $p$. Head sampling keeps each trace with probability $h$ before its outcome is known; the tail rule also keeps a share $t$ of the error traces. The chart plots against $t$ the error rate a dashboard computes over the kept traces (curve: large-sample value; dot: this sample), the design-weighted estimate that weights each kept trace by $1/\pi$, the inverse of its inclusion probability, and the population rate. With $t = 0$ both estimates are unbiased; any tail retention inflates the unweighted rate, most when $h$ is small. The population is seeded and the rates are illustrative."
```

### Replay has levels

An **exact replay** requires immutable model artifacts, prompts, index, tool
results, environment, and stochastic state. That is uncommon for hosted model
aliases and live tools. A **structural replay** reruns the same operation graph
against recorded or stubbed dependencies. A **semantic replay** asks whether the
new system still satisfies the case criterion despite different tokens or
steps.

Each replay is labeled with the fidelity it achieved. The record includes the
external state and the resolved provider revision, because a mutable model alias
is not reproducible evidence. A replay does not repeat a write, payment,
message, or other tool side effect to reproduce a trace; it uses an idempotent
sandbox, a recorded response, or an explicit dry-run adapter instead.

## Monitor a qualified release

An alert definition is a contract in the same sense as the release contract. It
records the metric revision, numerator, denominator, population and slices,
aggregation window, label delay, threshold, required duration, missing-data
rule, owner, and runbook, and the reference window and detector are versioned.
An alert without an owner and a tested response produces notifications that no
one acts on.

Monitoring covers at least:

- traffic mix, critical slices, and system-fingerprint integrity;
- trace completeness, missing telemetry, and schema validity;
- deterministic, task, security, and delayed human-label rates;
- judge output and disagreement between judge and human labels on a fixed
  anchor set, a locked human-labeled sample reused across releases;
- availability, end-to-end latency, tokens, and cost per accepted task.

End-to-end latency includes queueing, every retry, cache lookup, model call, and
tool call until an accepted result or terminal fallback. Cost per accepted task
includes failed attempts, judge cost, and allocated human review in addition to
the last completion.

A drift detector reports that a monitored distribution changed. Drift does not
identify the cause, prove that quality declined, or isolate the changed
component. Before a movement is attributed to a cause, trace integrity, traffic
mix, system revision, label delay, and evaluator stability are checked. A judge
whose scores change on the fixed human anchor set shows evaluator drift, which
can occur while the application itself is unchanged.

## Test failures before release

| Layer | Failure case | Required treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence | Holdout leakage, duplicate case, stale fingerprint | Invalidate the affected claim |
| Execution | Timeout, refusal, parser error, fallback | Preserve the outcome and denominator |
| Judge | Judge disagreement, order reversal, injected rubric override | Abstain, escalate, or disable the judge |
| Trace | Missing span, duplicate span, broken link, export failure | Mark completeness unknown; repair instrumentation |
| Sampling | Sampling bias, unknown inclusion probability, label nonresponse | Do not report an unweighted population rate |
| Privacy | Privacy leak, secret in baggage, cross-tenant trace | Hard stop, contain, delete, and investigate |
| Replay | Mutable model alias, changed external state, tool side effect | Downgrade fidelity; use a sandbox or recording |
| Rollout | Critical-slice regression, latency breach, runaway cost | Stop ramp and restore last-known-good |

## Operate the release lifecycle

1. Freeze the decision, system fingerprint, population, slices, metrics, and
   privacy boundary.
2. Version the dataset manifest, provenance, consent basis, labels, and split
   assignment.
3. Declare cases, independent units, repeated trials, weights, invalid outcomes,
   and uncertainty method.
4. Qualify every human protocol and model judge against appropriate reference
   evidence.
5. Run baseline and candidate under matched conditions; retain every attempt.
6. Apply hard constraints and confidence-bound gates to every required slice.
7. Use shadow execution where it can reveal integration faults without user
   effects, then start a small sticky canary.
8. Ramp only while quality, security, latency, cost, and telemetry-completeness
   stop rules pass.
9. Roll back atomically to the last-known-good revision when a rollback trigger
   fires.
10. Store estimates, intervals, invalid outcomes, waivers, approvals, canary
    results, expiry, rollback target, and each requalification trigger.

Steps 5 and 6 run in CI on every change. In the minimal Promptfoo configuration
below, the harness and the judge reach models only through the model gateway
(@sec-wiring-stack), each with its own budget-capped key, and a deterministic
check runs before the judge so that cheap failures cost no judge call. The model
names are gateway aliases, and the judge alias routes to a different model
family from the system under test.

```yaml
# promptfooconfig.yaml
providers:
  - id: openai:chat:smart              # gateway alias for the system under test
    config:
      apiBaseUrl: https://llm-gateway.internal/v1
      apiKeyEnvar: EVAL_GATEWAY_KEY    # the harness's own scoped key
prompts:
  - "Using only the context, answer as JSON with fields answer and citations.\n{{context}}\n\nQ: {{question}}"
tests:
  - vars: { question: "...", context: "..." }
    assert:
      - type: is-json                  # deterministic check, runs first
      - type: llm-rubric               # a qualified model judge
        value: "Every claim in the answer is supported by a cited context passage."
        provider:
          id: openai:chat:judge        # gateway alias, a different model family
          config:
            apiBaseUrl: https://llm-gateway.internal/v1
            apiKeyEnvar: JUDGE_GATEWAY_KEY
```

The CI step is one command, `npx promptfoo@latest eval -c promptfooconfig.yaml
--no-cache -o results.json`. It exits with status 100 when any test fails or
the pass rate falls below `PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD`, so the pipeline fails
without further scripting [@promptfoo2026cli]. This per-test gate complements
the statistical gate above: the configuration catches known failures on
individual cases, and the paired comparison with its interval decides whether
the candidate as a whole is non-inferior.

The output is an evaluation release record. It binds the claim and evidence to
the exact system that was released, explains uncertainty and unresolved slices,
and makes recovery executable.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

The serving architecture constrains what can be evaluated and replayed. Stable
component identifiers, scoped evaluator credentials, metering, and a gateway or
equivalent routing record make paired comparison safer. Trace completeness and
judge validity are established separately, by the trace contract and by judge
qualification.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

How much judgment to automate remains unsettled. Deterministic checks are
precise but narrow; model judges scale but inherit bias and attack surface;
human reviewers add expertise along with disagreement, selection effects, and
delay. Each method suits the criteria it can support. Whatever the mix,
abstention and uncertainty stay in the record, and the release record names the
evidence the decision rested on.
:::
